newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Main points of new South Korean labour law.
newsitem.headline: Main points of new South Korean labour law.

text.p: At the root of South Korea's current labour strife is a controversial labour law which the ruling New Korea Party rammed through parliament on December 26.
Passage of the law at a dawn meeting from which the opposition was missing led to wildcat strikes that culminated with calls for an all-out stoppage starting on Tuesday.
The government sanctions only one umbrella union called the Federation of Korean Trade Unions, which has 1.2 million members out of a workforce of 12 million.
The outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions has 500,000 members.
Following are the main points of controversy in the law, which takes effect on March 1, taken from a briefing summary released by the Ministry of Labour:
-- Firms can dismiss workers for urgent managerial reasons such as company restructuring, technological innovation to boost productivity and mergers and acquisitions.
-- Multiple trade unions will be allowed at national and industrial sector level from 2000 and at a company level from 2002.
-- Postponement of allowing teachers to form unions.

-- Companies can replace striking workers with non-union company staff. If no non-union workers are available and companies are likely to suffer serious financial loss, outside workers can be hired temporarily with permission from an independent labour commission.
-- Employers shall not pay employees on strike.
-- Ban lifted on third party intervention in collective bargaining and strikes. But unions will have to report to the labour minister who such parties will be.
-- Article prohibiting trade union involvement in political activity abolished, provided a union's primary objective is not political.

-- Introduction of flexible working hours to allow a 48-hour week on condition average working hours over a two-week period do not exceed 44 hours per week. If written agreement is reached between employers and workers, maximum weekly hours can be extended to 56 hours, but with the same 44-hour average.
-- From 2002 companies shall not pay full-time union officials.
